name: Vale
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.note: No grammar or phonology of Vale (CAR) located online

tone_statements.citation: Olson, Kenneth S. 2024. A preliminary phonology of Vale. In Yaqian Huang, Nina Hagen Kaldhol, Jun Jie Lim, Sharon Rose & Anthony Struthers-Young (eds.), ACAL in SoCAL: Selected papers from the 53rd Annual Conference on African Linguistics, 455–474. Berlin: Language Science Press. DOI 10.5281/zenodo.11210474
tone_statements.quote: It has two level tones, and I posit five underlying tone melodies: L, H, LH, HL, and HLH. All of these melodies occur on monomorphemic words. The L in the HLH pattern is realized as a floating L which triggers non-automatic downstep, so the HLH pattern surfaces as HꜜH. [...] 5 Tone. Vale has two unambiguous tone levels, which I label as High (H) and Low (L). Words demonstrating the contrast between these two levels are shown in Table 9. [...] From the perspective of moraic theory, this means that CVV syllables have two moras and the tone bearing unit (TBU) in Vale is the mora.
tone_statements.locator: abstract p. 455; TBU statement (end of §4) and §5 'Tone' opening sentence both on p. 463 (not 462); five-melody conclusion p. 467
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone_statements.n_tones: 2 level (H, L) + non-automatic downstep; 5 underlying melodies L/H/LH/HL/HLH

tone_statements.citation: Olson, Kenneth S. 2022. A preliminary phonology of Vale. Abstract, 53rd Annual Conference on African Linguistics (ACAL 53), University of California San Diego, April 2022. 1 p.
tone_statements.quote: Vale has two contrastive level tones, H and L. Monomoraic words take either a H or L tone. Bimoraic words have one of five surface tonal patterns: LL, HH, LH, HL, or HꜜH. This system resembles the Proto Sara-Bongo-Bagirmi system posited by Boyeldieu (2006:10–11), which also had two level tones (H and L) and five tonal patterns: LL, HH, LH, HL(a), and HL(b). Preliminary evidence suggests that downstep [ꜜ] in Vale results from a floating L tone.

tone.says: §5 Tone runs pp. 463–467 (S wrote 462–467); content of S's summary otherwise stands: two level tones H/L, TBU = mora, apparent Superhigh-High pattern reanalysed as /HLH/ with floating L and non-automatic downstep, five underlying melodies L/H/LH/HL/HLH on monomorphemic words, downstep across words via HLH Plateauing, comparison with Boyeldieu's Proto-SBB two-tone system; no stress statement.

sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: not located online or in the libraries checked
sources.note: Nothing on stress/accent; ch. IV 'Tonématique' (p. 61 ff.) states 'Le vâlé, à l'instar des langues africaines, est une langue à ton' and inventories 3 level tones (H, M, B) + 2 contour tones. Identity doubtful: Olson 2024: 469–470 argues this 'Vale de Ndélé' is probably Luto (Ndoka or Wad) rather than Vale.

sources.note: States two contrastive level tones H and L; monomoraic words H or L; bimoraic words show five surface patterns LL, HH, LH, HL, HꜜH; downstep from a floating L (e.g. /jé.lè/ + /kú.lí/ -> [jé.ꜜlé kú.lí] 'cool wind', HLH Plateauing); proposes five underlying melodies /L, H, LH, HL, HLH/, compared with Boyeldieu's (2006) Proto-SBB two-tone system and with Siane (PNG).
